what_it_does: Neutral atom quantum computers are a type of quantum hardware where individual atoms, trapped in place by focused laser beams, serve as quantum bits (qubits — the quantum equivalent of a classical 0/1 bit). Unlike some quantum hardware, these atoms can be physically moved between different regions (zones) of the device to carry out different types of operations. Compiling a quantum algorithm onto this hardware requires simultaneously deciding which gates (quantum operations) to run, where each qubit-atom should physically sit, when and how to move atoms between zones, and how to handle communication across zones — a massively combinatorial scheduling problem that existing compilers solve poorly. PowerMove is a compiler that treats atom movement as a central optimization target rather than an afterthought, jointly scheduling gates, positions, and moves together. It also covers fault-tolerant quantum computing, where instead of working with raw physical qubits you encode each logical qubit across many physical qubits using quantum error-correcting codes, and applies the same joint optimization. The paper reports up to 216x speedup in compilation time relative to prior tools.
